newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Foreign insurers would not crush Asian firms -exec.
newsitem.headline: Foreign insurers would not crush Asian firms -exec.

text.p: Foreign firms are not intent on crushing Asia's fledgling insurance companies, a senior western executive said on Thursday after the Indian parliament rejected legislation to let them into the country.

"Foreign companies are not the big bad wolf that is going to take away business and jobs," said Patrick Dutrey, Asia Pacific regional vice president for France's Axa-UAP, told Reuters in an interview.
On Wednesday, India rejected legislation that would have allowed foreign firms to enter the state-controlled insurance sector.
"We need to find a way to disseminate information to show that we will bring in capital and experience and create jobs," he said.
Axa-UAP, Europe's biggest insurer with global premium income of Ffr340 billion in 1996, had pinned many of its hopes for expansion in Asia on India as well as China.

The company, which has its Asia regional headquarters in Singapore, had been searching for a local partner to enter India's health insurance sector -- flagged to have been first to open to foreign firms -- and had 1998 as its tentative start date.
"When will we get there now? The dates would be purely wishful thinking. I could tell you by the next budget, but that would be completely pointless," Dutrey said.
"We thought it (the legislation) would go through this time, but this is a real setback," he added.

Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral was forced to withdraw legislation to allow foreign firms to enter India's insurance market after failing to muster enough parliamentary support to keep the Insurance Regulatory Authority Bill alive.
The bill would have created a body to oversee the state-run insurance industry and was seen as a first step towards the eventual opening up of the sector to competition.
It was introduced in July by Finance Minister P Chidambaram, 3-1/2 years after far reaching reform of insurance was recommended by the government-appointed Malhotra Committee.
But Dutrey said he was hopeful the setback was not a permanent block to liberalisation of India's insurance sector.

"The Ministry of Finance is very pro opening the financial sector, so there is something to work from there. We now have to realise that this is going to take longer than we anticipated or would like," he said.
"What we could do and should do now is to allay the fears of the people involved -- the General Insurance Corporation, the politicians and the unions," Dutrey said.
